section.title: Signs of the Coming Siege
section.sectionRationale: Before Ezekiel speaks a single oracle in his own words, God turns him into a walking sermon: a brick city under siege, hundreds of days lying bound on his side, rationed bread and water, and finally a shaved head with its hair burned, struck, and scattered. Each act pictures, in miniature, what is about to happen to Jerusalem in full.
section.thesis: Through humiliating, costly sign acts performed on his own body, Ezekiel dramatizes the certainty and severity of the coming siege and fall of Jerusalem, showing that the city's judgment answers real, prolonged rebellion against a God who had set her above every nation.
section.frameNote: Four scenes: the brick city under siege; bearing Israel's and Judah's iniquity by lying bound for hundreds of days; the rationed, defiled bread and water; and the shaved hair divided by fire, sword, and wind, with the oracle of judgment it pictures.

units.label: The brick city under siege
units.note: a sign to the house of Israel

verses.text: “Now you, son of man, take a brick, place it before you, and draw on it the city of Jerusalem.
Then lay siege against it: Construct a siege wall, build a ramp to it, set up camps against it, and place battering rams around it on all sides.
Then take an iron plate and set it up as an iron wall between yourself and the city. Turn your face toward it so that it is under siege, and besiege it. This will be a sign to the house of Israel.
Then lie down on your left side and place the {{avon|iniquity}} of the house of Israel upon yourself. You are to bear their iniquity for the number of days you lie on your side.
For I have assigned to you 390 days, according to the number of years of their iniquity. So you shall bear the iniquity of the house of Israel.
When you have completed these days, lie down again, but on your right side, and bear the iniquity of the house of Judah. I have assigned to you 40 days, a day for each year.
You must turn your face toward the siege of Jerusalem with your arm bared, and prophesy against it.
Now behold, I will tie you up with ropes so you cannot turn from side to side until you have finished the days of your siege.

units.label: Rationed bread and defiled water
units.note: eating and drinking the siege itself

verses.text: But take wheat, barley, beans, lentils, millet, and spelt; put them in a single container and make them into bread for yourself. This is what you are to eat during the 390 days you lie on your side.
You are to weigh out twenty shekels of food to eat each day, and you are to eat it at set times.
You are also to measure out a sixth of a hin of water to drink, and you are to drink it at set times.
And you shall eat the food as you would a barley cake, after you bake it over dried human excrement in the sight of the people.”
Then the LORD said, “This is how the Israelites will eat their defiled bread among the nations to which I will banish them.”
“Ah, Lord GOD,” I said, “I have never defiled myself. From my youth until now I have not eaten anything found dead or mauled by wild beasts. No unclean meat has ever entered my mouth.”
“Look,” He replied, “I will let you use cow dung instead of human excrement, and you may bake your bread over that.”
Then He told me, “Son of man, I am going to cut off the supply of food in Jerusalem. They will anxiously eat bread rationed by weight, and in despair they will drink water by measure.
So they will lack food and water; they will be appalled at the sight of one another wasting away in their iniquity.

units.label: The shaved hair, divided by fire, sword, and wind
units.note: a third burned, a third struck, a third scattered

verses.text: “As for you, son of man, take a sharp sword, use it as a barber's razor, and shave your head and beard. Then take a set of scales and divide the hair.

When the days of the siege have ended, you are to burn up a third of the hair inside the city; you are also to take a third and slash it with the sword all around the city; and you are to scatter a third to the wind. For I will unleash a sword behind them.
But you are to take a few strands of hair and secure them in the folds of your garment.
Again, take a few of these, throw them into the fire, and burn them. From there a fire will spread to the whole house of Israel.
This is what the Lord GOD says: ‘This is Jerusalem, which I have set in the center of the nations, with countries all around her.

But she has rebelled against My ordinances more wickedly than the nations, and against My statutes worse than the countries around her. For her people have rejected My ordinances and have not walked in My statutes.’

Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘You have been more insubordinate than the nations around you; you have not walked in My statutes or kept My ordinances, nor have you even conformed to the ordinances of the nations around you.’
Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Behold, I Myself am against you, Jerusalem, and I will execute judgments among you in the sight of the nations.
Because of all your abominations, I will do to you what I have never done before and will never do again.
As a result, fathers among you will eat their sons, and sons will eat their fathers. I will execute judgments against you and scatter all your remnant to every wind.’

Therefore as surely as I live, declares the Lord GOD, because you have defiled My sanctuary with all your detestable idols and abominations, I Myself will withdraw My favor; I will not look upon you with pity, nor will I spare you.

A third of your people will die by plague or be consumed by famine within you, a third will fall by the sword outside your walls, and a third I will scatter to every wind and unleash a sword behind them.
And when My anger is spent and I have vented My wrath against them, I will be appeased. And when I have spent My wrath on them, they will know that I, the LORD, in My zeal have spoken.
I will make you a ruin and a disgrace among the nations around you, in the sight of all who pass by.
So you will be a reproach and a taunt, a warning and a horror to the nations around you, when I execute judgments against you in anger, wrath, and raging fury. I, the LORD, have spoken.
When I shower you with the deadly arrows of famine and destruction that I will send to destroy you, I will intensify the famine against you and cut off your supply of food.
I will send famine and wild beasts against you, and they will leave you childless. Plague and bloodshed will sweep through you, and I will bring a sword against you. I, the LORD, have spoken.”

avon.gloss: Iniquity, guilt, the twisted weight of sin and its punishment together. Ezekiel is told to bear this avon on his own body, day for year, a costly, symbolic picture of a burden the people themselves refuse to feel or confess.

basic.context: Before Ezekiel speaks a single sermon, God makes his very body into a sign. He draws Jerusalem on a clay brick and lays siege to it in miniature. He lies bound on his side for over a year, bearing Israel's and Judah's iniquity day for year. He eats meager, defiled bread and drinks rationed water, exactly as the besieged city will do. Finally he shaves his head and beard and divides the hair three ways, burned, struck, and scattered, a living picture of what will happen to Jerusalem's people when the siege finally breaks the city.
basic.hermeneutics: These are prophetic sign acts, a well-known Old Testament form in which the prophet's own actions dramatize the coming word of God; they are meant to be read as vivid, costly performance rather than literal instructions for later readers to imitate. The point is not the mechanics of numbers and rationing but the certainty and severity of the judgment they portray, and the real rebellion that has made it necessary.
basic.originalLanguages: Ezekiel bears Israel's avon, iniquity, physically, a word that binds together guilt and its punishment as one weight. The oracle explains that Jerusalem has outdone even the pagan nations in rebellion against the ordinances she alone was given, reaching the limit of God's patience.
basic.typology: Ezekiel bearing the iniquity of Israel and Judah on his own body, lying bound and afflicted for their sake, dimly foreshadows the far greater Servant who would actually bear the iniquity of His people, not merely in symbol but in fact, on the cross.
basic.christ: Isaiah's Suffering Servant, who bears our iniquities and is bound and afflicted for us, deepens what Ezekiel's sign act only pictures, and Christ fulfills it fully: He alone truly bears the sin of His people, not for a set number of symbolic days but once for all upon the cross, so that the judgment threatened here need never fall on those who are found in Him.
basic.god: God is patient enough to warn a whole city in advance through years of enacted sign, yet He is also just: Jerusalem's rebellion has exceeded the nations around her, so that the judgment, when it falls, is neither arbitrary nor sudden but the fitting outcome of persistent unfaithfulness.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 53:4-6 describes the Servant bearing iniquity in a way Ezekiel's sign act only foreshadows. Leviticus 26:27-29 already warned of siege cannibalism as covenant curse, now realized in Ezekiel 5:10. 2 Kings 25 records the literal fall of Jerusalem this section predicts.
basic.oneStory: This is the moment the covenant curses long threatened in the Law become an unavoidable, embodied warning: judgment is coming because rebellion has run its course. Yet even here, a man bearing others' iniquity in his own body points forward to the true Bearer of iniquity, Jesus Christ, whose suffering ends the judgment His people deserved.

context.literary:
The section is a run of four acted sermons, each built the same way: a command to do something, the staging of it, and then a word from God that interprets it. The brick and iron plate come first, 4:1-3, and close with the plain label 'This will be a sign to the house of Israel.' The long lying on his side follows, 4:4-8, then the weighed bread and measured water, 4:9-17, and last the razor and the scales, 5:1-4, with the interpretation of that final act running on through 5:5-17. Notice that the first three acts are explained in a few lines of rationing and hunger, while the fourth gets a full oracle. The sign is silent theatre; the oracle is what the audience must be made to hear.

The acts also tighten as they go. The brick is a model, the lying is an ordeal, the bread is a hardship, and the razor is a loss, since a priest's hair and beard were not lightly cut. Each step moves from picture to the prophet's own flesh. This follows the muting of 3:25-27, where Ezekiel is bound with ropes and kept from speaking except when God opens his mouth, so for now he can only act.

Chapter 5 is arranged in thirds. The hair is divided in thirds, 5:2, and the oracle repeats the three fates in 5:12, plague and famine inside, sword outside, scattering beyond. A few strands are saved in his garment and then some of those are thrown on the fire, 5:3-4. The heart of the oracle is 5:8, 'Behold, I Myself am against you, Jerusalem,' and the refrain 'I, the LORD, have spoken' closes 5:13, 5:15 and 5:17. The famine and sword and beasts and plague of 5:12-17 are the four judgments the prophet names again in 14:21.
context.historical:
Ezekiel was a priest, 1:3, deported with King Jehoiachin in 597 BC, 2 Kings 24:14-16, and these acts belong to the years after his call in the fifth year of that exile, 1:2, and before the siege itself began, which Ezekiel marks with a date in 24:1-2. His audience were fellow exiles at Tel-abib, 3:15, many of them sure that the stay in Babylon was short and that Jerusalem, with its temple and its Davidic king in Zedekiah's place, could not fall. Prophets at home were saying the same, Jeremiah 14:13-14. A brick with a city scratched on it would have looked, to such a crowd, like madness or like a child's game, and that is why the sign had to be done where people could watch, 4:12.

The details of the siege were not guesswork. Ancient armies used exactly what 4:2 lists: a siege wall, a ramp, camps and rams. The real siege, when it came, began on the tenth day of the tenth month of Zedekiah's ninth year and ended when the city was breached in the fourth month of his eleventh year, 2 Kings 25:1-4 and Jeremiah 52:4-6, about eighteen months, with famine so severe that the people of the land had no food.

The rationing is arithmetic, not poetry. The BSB notes that twenty shekels of food is about eight ounces, and a sixth of a hin of water about two thirds of a quart, enough to stay alive and no more, 4:10-11. The grain list in 4:9 is what a household scrapes together when the pantry is nearly bare. The curses behind 5:10 were old: parents eating children in a siege is threatened in Leviticus 26:29 and Deuteronomy 28:53, and the Bible records it happening, Lamentations 4:10 and 2:20.
context.canonical:
Ezekiel's acts take their place in a family of prophetic signs. Isaiah walked stripped and barefoot for three years as a sign against Egypt and Cush, Isaiah 20:2-4. Jeremiah wore a linen loincloth he buried and found rotted, Jeremiah 13:1, and wore a yoke, Jeremiah 27:2. Hosea's marriage and Isaiah's children's names were signs too, Hosea 1 and Isaiah 8:3. Ezekiel's own cycle includes the packing of exile baggage and digging through a wall in 12:1-7, and the silence at his wife's death in chapter 24. What sets these acts apart is how much they cost the body.

The passage leans on the covenant. The sword that God will 'unleash' behind the scattered, 5:2, 5:12, is Leviticus 26:33, and the rationed bread by weight in 4:16 is Leviticus 26:26. The forty days a day for a year match the sentence of Numbers 14:34. The line about doing 'what I have never done before and will never do again,' 5:9, is picked up in Lamentations 4:6, where Jerusalem's punishment is greater than Sodom's, and in Jesus' warning of a tribulation never seen before, Matthew 24:21.

The New Testament hears the whole drama again. Jesus wept over Jerusalem and described the barricade, the ring of enemies and not one stone left on another, Luke 19:41-44, and told His followers to flee when they saw the city surrounded by armies, Luke 21:20. Peter's reply in Acts 10:14, 'I have never eaten anything impure or unclean,' is almost Ezekiel's protest of 4:14 on a Gentile's doorstep, and the answer in Acts 10:15 reverses the defiled bread of 4:13.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Ezekiel wanted the exiles to give up a particular comfort: the belief that Jerusalem's fall could not happen to them, or could not happen soon. A sermon can be argued with, but a man lying bound in the road for months cannot be argued with. The prophet's body becomes the evidence that God means what He says, and that He is prepared to spend a servant's health and dignity to be believed.

The oracle of 5:5-17 explains why. Jerusalem was set 'in the center of the nations,' 5:5, to show them what life under God's statutes looked like, and instead she did worse than the nations around her, 5:6-7. The accusation is not that she was ordinary but that she had received more and returned less. So the exiles are also asked to see their own part. They are not victims of an unlucky war; they are hearing the verdict of a God who has been patient, who warned in advance, and who now acts openly.

There is a mercy tucked inside the severity. The warning is given years before the siege begins. People who see the brick and hear the explanation have time to understand, to stop trusting the city, and to hold the Lord's word when it comes true. The few hairs tucked into the garment, 5:3, and the survivors promised elsewhere, 14:22, keep the door open for a people who will be there to listen afterward.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The text describes commands given to one priest-prophet in one crisis. No one is told to lie on one side for a year, to bake bread over dung, or to shave the head and burn the hair. The prophets who copied such acts did so only when God told them, and the acts were always aimed at the audience, not at the prophet's own devotion. Reading the passage as a model of sacrifice for the sake of a message, or as a pattern for dramatic protest, misses that every act here was ordered and interpreted by God.

The verses that do carry forward are statements. God is against a people who corrupt His gifts, 5:8. He warns before He strikes. His judgments are public so that others learn from them, 5:8 and 5:15. And God remains the one who lets a servant's honest protest change the terms: when Ezekiel objects to the human excrement, God grants cow dung instead, 4:15. Believers can take from that a freedom to pray plainly about the cost of obedience without treating obedience as negotiable.

The cannibalism of 5:10 is recorded as a curse that was feared and later suffered, not as something God approves. The text reports it as the end of covenant breaking, which the law had foretold and Lamentations mourns.

debates.question: What do the 390 days and the 40 days stand for?

views.label: Years of the northern and southern kingdoms' guilt
views.case: The text pairs each day with a year of iniquity, 4:5-6, and puts the 390 on Israel and the 40 on Judah. Some count from a point in the monarchy to the exile, and take the two figures as the length of the sin or the punishment of each house. Judah's forty also recalls the forty years of Numbers 14:34, where each day of spying became a year of bearing guilt.

views.label: A total of 430, echoing Egypt
views.case: Added together the figures give 430, the length of Israel's stay in Egypt, Exodus 12:40-41. On this reading Ezekiel is told that the exile is a return to bondage, the old story played backward, and the sign is about a fresh slavery rather than a calendar.

views.label: Round numbers whose point is the burden itself
views.case: Some prefer not to settle a start date at all. The numbers are large and exact enough to be felt, and Ezekiel gives no calendar from which to count. What matters is that guilt is measured, tallied and borne, not that readers can match each figure to a king.

debates.bearing: All three agree that the numbers are deliberate and that they speak of guilt that was counted. The text itself explains the day-for-year scale, so it is wiser to ride that explanation than to build a timetable from it.

debates.question: Did Ezekiel really lie on his side for more than a year, or is the account a vision or literary report?

views.label: He did it literally, in public
views.case: The commands are physical and the verbs are plain: tied with ropes, 4:8, weighed bread, 4:10, baking 'in the sight of the people,' 4:12. His objection of 4:14 sounds like a man facing a real meal. The obvious reading is that exiles watched him and the weeks were counted.

views.label: Perhaps in part, or in stages
views.case: Some note practical strains, such as a single man bound for 430 days while still attending to the daily needs of life, and suggest the acts were done at intervals, for stretches of each day, or that some were performed in vision, as the temple tour of chapter 8 certainly was.

views.label: A literary arrangement of what he did and said
views.case: Others think the written chapter gathers several enactments into one scroll, shaped for readers, without every detail being a day-by-day record.

debates.bearing: The text claims public enactment and gives no hint that readers should doubt it, so the plain reading deserves the first hearing. The message does not depend on settling the mechanics, since in every case the point is the same: God made His word visible in His servant.

study.originalLanguages:
The most important verb in this section is the one for bearing. In 4:4-6 Ezekiel is told to 'bear' the iniquity of Israel and then of Judah, from the verb nasa, 'lift up, carry.' It is the verb of priestly duty. Aaron wears the plate on his forehead 'so that he may bear the iniquity of the holy things,' Exodus 28:38, and priests are told in Numbers 18:1 that they must bear the iniquity involving the sanctuary. It is also the verb of the scapegoat, which 'will carry on itself all their iniquities' into the wilderness, Leviticus 16:22. Ezekiel is a priest, 1:3, and the language puts him in the ritual role of one who lifts sin off a people and carries it away. The difference is that the people see no sin removed. Here the bearing is a sign of how heavy their guilt is, not a way of taking it off. In Isaiah 53:12 the same verb turns up in 'He bore the sin of many,' where the bearing is real and effective.

The word for what he is doing is a 'sign,' 4:3, in Hebrew ot, the same word used for the rainbow, Genesis 9:12, and for the wonders in Egypt. Later in the book Ezekiel is also called a mofet, a 'portent' or 'wonder,' as in 12:6 and 24:24. An ot points to something beyond itself, and the iron plate set between Ezekiel and the city is a sign of exactly that kind: a wall of separation, 4:3, as if God Himself had turned His face against Jerusalem.

The protest of 4:14 is carefully worded. The BSB footnote notes that the Hebrew has Ezekiel saying 'my soul,' nephesh, has never been defiled. He also says he has never eaten meat that was piggul. That word belongs to the priestly law and describes sacrificial meat left past the time it could be eaten, Leviticus 19:7, and the sense of 'foul' or 'rejected' clings to it. His claim is about priestly purity, which Leviticus 22:8 spells out when it forbids priests to eat anything found dead or torn by beasts. God does not argue; He changes the fuel.

In 4:16 the BSB translates 'bread rationed by weight,' but the footnote gives the Hebrew as 'staff,' the staff of bread, bread as what holds a person upright. Breaking the staff is the same language as Leviticus 26:26. A few verses later, 5:16, the footnote tells the same story, so the famine is not an accident but a repeated image of support removed.

The hardest line is 5:13: 'I will be appeased.' The Hebrew verb is nacham, usually 'comfort' or 'relent.' Here it means God's anger, spent, is quieted. The same verb comes back in 14:22, where survivors will be 'comforted' about the disaster once they see what happened. It is a hint that the end of wrath is not the end of the story.

Finally, 'I Myself am against you,' 5:8, uses a formula of challenge, 'Behold, I am against you,' that God aims at proud enemies such as Babylon in Jeremiah 50:31 and Pharaoh in Ezekiel 29:3. Turning it on Jerusalem is a shock: the city has become the enemy it was meant to be rescued from.

typology.type: The prophet-priest bearing the people's iniquity, Ezekiel 4:4-6
typology.fulfillment: Ezekiel lies on one side and then the other, bound with ropes, carrying the guilt of two houses in picture. The picture is a priestly one, since priests bore iniquity, Numbers 18:1, and the scapegoat carried sins away, Leviticus 16:22. Christ is the priest who bears sin in fact: 'He Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree,' 1 Peter 2:24, 'offered once to bear the sins of many,' Hebrews 9:28. The escalation is that His bearing removes what Ezekiel's only displays. The type falls short because Ezekiel's days ended and the guilt remained, while Christ's bearing ends the debt for His people.

The brick city under siege is a picture of a city shut up in judgment. Jesus saw it coming a second time. He wept over Jerusalem and said her enemies would barricade her and hem her in, Luke 19:41-44, and He named the armies encircling the city as the sign to flee, Luke 21:20. The temple that Ezekiel's hearers thought untouchable was left 'desolate,' Matthew 23:38. The pattern repeats because the cause repeats: Jerusalem did not recognize the time of her visitation. Where it falls short is that Ezekiel's siege led to exile and return, while the rejection of the Messiah brought a judgment tied to a greater fulfilment.

typology.type: Defiled bread among the nations, Ezekiel 4:13
typology.fulfillment: God says Israel will eat defiled bread among the nations where He banishes them. Exile makes the clean life of the covenant impossible, so food itself becomes an emblem of banishment. The gospel unlocks the other side: Jesus declared all foods clean, Mark 7:19, and Peter learned in the vision at Joppa not to call impure what God has made clean, Acts 10:14-15, just as the gospel reached Gentile homes. The correspondence is that the exile that spread Israel among the nations prepared the way for the nations to hear. It is an echo, not a stated fulfilment, but it shows that the curse of scattering was turned into a channel of blessing.

typology.type: The few hairs saved and then burned, Ezekiel 5:3-4
typology.fulfillment: A small number of hairs are saved in the garment, then some of those are thrown into the fire. The picture says that even the remnant is not safe by being a remnant. A holy seed remains as a stump after the felling, Isaiah 6:13, and Paul speaks of 'a remnant chosen by grace,' Romans 11:5, a remnant secured by God's choice and not by the survivors' merit. In Christ the remnant is gathered into one person who passed through the fire of judgment and came out alive. The type falls short because Ezekiel's few strands are still at risk, while those found in Christ are not.

study.christ:
This section does not name the Messiah, and it would be a mistake to push the text further than it goes. What it does is make a promise sound heavier. The priest-prophet carries iniquity, the people are hit by the consequences, and the reader is left asking how a guilt of this size could ever be lifted. The rest of Scripture gives the answer in a Person.

The first link is the verb of bearing. Ezekiel's work belongs to the priests, who bore the iniquity of the holy things, Exodus 28:38, and to the goat that carried the sins of Israel into the wilderness, Leviticus 16:22. Jesus is the priest and the sacrifice together. Hebrews says He was 'offered once to bear the sins of many,' Hebrews 9:28, and Peter says He bore our sins 'in His body on the tree,' 1 Peter 2:24, wording that picks up the bodily nature of Ezekiel's acts. Where Ezekiel's body was a sign of a burden he could not remove, the body of Christ was the place where it was removed. Hebrews also notes that Jesus suffered outside the city gate, 13:11-13, as the sin offering was burned outside the camp. Ezekiel's hair, burned in the city and slashed and scattered around it, 5:2, shows what happens to a people who stay inside the walls of judgment, and the gospel's answer is a Man who went outside the city to take that judgment.

The second link is the mourning over Jerusalem. The siege Ezekiel scratched on a brick is what Jesus describes with tears, Luke 19:41-44. The Lord of the temple speaks the same verdict that Ezekiel was ordered to act out, and speaks it grieving. Notice that He does not cheer for the siege. Ezekiel was commanded to pronounce the sentence, but Jesus is the one who lays down His life for the same city. His cry, 'If only you had known on this day what would bring you peace!', is the compassion that the severity of Ezekiel 5 was always meant to lead to.

The third link concerns hunger. Ezekiel eats by weight and drinks by measure. Jesus feeds crowds with more than enough and calls Himself the bread of life, John 6:35, and the Lord's Supper turns bread into the sign of a body given. The scarcity of Ezekiel's rations is the curse of covenant breaking, and abundance in Christ is its reversal. Isaiah 55:2 asks why anyone should spend on what is not bread, and invites all to eat what is good.

A caution is needed. The acts are not a riddle about Jesus in which each brick stands for a part of His life. The links rest on the shared language of bearing, the New Testament's own use of the Servant, and Jesus' own words over the city. What Ezekiel's signs supply is the weight of the problem, so that the cross can be seen for what it carries.
study.god:
The first thing the section shows is a God who warns. He does not spring the siege on a sleeping city; He spends years of one man's life to tell it. Judgment arrives long after the notice, and the notice is made impossible to miss: a drawing on a brick, a body bound in public, a razor and a pair of scales. Elsewhere He swears that He takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, Ezekiel 18:23 and 33:11, and the length of this warning is of a piece with that oath. A God who wants people to turn does not hide the sentence.

He is also a God of searching, measured justice. The oracle of 5:5-7 says that Jerusalem's guilt is greater precisely because of her privilege: she was placed in the center of the nations, with the ordinances and statutes, and she kept neither. God weighs people by what they were given. The same standard appears in Amos 3:2 and in Jesus' words about cities that saw miracles and did not repent. The thirds of 5:12 and the scales of 5:1 present a justice that is exact: nothing lost in the wrath, nothing missing from the verdict.

He is jealous and personal. 'I Myself am against you,' 5:8, is not the language of a distant force. And 5:11 says He will 'withdraw My favor' because they defiled His sanctuary; the cause is not national misfortune but the holiness of God who dwells among His people. The sanctuary is the thing that makes the city precious, and so its defilement is what makes it vulnerable.

There is a tension here that the passage does not resolve and does not need to. God's wrath is terrible, 5:13-17, and yet it is 'spent,' and when it is spent He is 'appeased.' His anger is not a mood that wanders; it is a settled response to evil that comes to an end. The survivors scattered to every wind, 5:10, are not forgotten, since a few hairs are saved in the garment, 5:3, and the book promises that those who escape will remember Him, 6:8-10 and 14:22. Judgment and a remnant are held in one hand.

He is, finally, a God who listens to His servant. In 4:14 Ezekiel pleads from his priestly conscience and the Lord gives way on the fuel without giving way on the sign. The One who commands is not deaf to the one who obeys.

For worship, this means taking warnings as gifts. The right response to a God who speaks in advance is not defiance or panic but attention. A people who have been told the truth about the cost of sin can still repent, and the God who tells them is the God who will one day be 'a sanctuary for them,' 11:16, in the very countries to which they are sent.

crossReferences.note: The Lord had threatened to cut off the supply of bread so that ten women would bake in a single oven and ration the loaves by weight. Ezekiel's measured bread in 4:16 is that old warning enacted. The covenant had already spelled out what rebellion would cost, which is why the sign could not be dismissed as a novelty.

Parents eating their children, high places destroyed, and corpses piled on the remains of idols are in this chapter of covenant curses. Ezekiel 5:10 and 6:4-5 turn those curses from threat into announcement. Together they show that Ezekiel does not invent new judgments; he reads the old treaty aloud.

A year of bearing guilt for each day of the spies' trip: forty days, forty years. Ezekiel's day for a year in 4:5-6 draws on this exchange rate, and the forty days for Judah echo the wilderness generation. The same God who fixed one sentence in the desert fixes another in Babylon.

On the Day of Atonement the priest lays Israel's iniquities on the goat's head, and the goat carries them away. Ezekiel's 'bearing' of iniquity borrows this ritual language, but with no sin removed, only displayed. The contrast makes the later fulfilment clearer.

Isaiah walked naked and barefoot for three years as a sign against Egypt and Cush. It is the nearest Old Testament parallel to Ezekiel's ordeal, a prophet who lets the message cost him his dignity. Both are living illustrations of what armies will do to captives.

The historical record of the siege Ezekiel enacts: Nebuchadnezzar's camp, the siege wall built around the city, and a famine so severe that the people had no food. Reading Ezekiel 4 beside this passage shows how closely the drama anticipated the facts.

The hands of compassionate women cooked their own children. This is the grief poet's report of the fulfilment of Ezekiel 5:10 and Leviticus 26:29. It shows how literally the curse came true and why the prophet was commanded to stage it with such severity.

God names again the four judgments of sword, famine, wild beasts and plague, but now adds that survivors will be left who will come out to the exiles. The same verb that appears in 5:13 for God being 'appeased' appears here for the survivors being 'comforted,' so the judgment of chapter 5 is not the last word.

Jesus weeps over Jerusalem and describes the barricade, the encirclement and the leveling. He echoes Ezekiel's drawn siege with eyes wet, giving the brick a second meaning. The city that Ezekiel was told to besiege in model is the city that Jesus mourns.

Peter protests that he has never eaten anything impure or unclean, nearly repeating Ezekiel's words in 4:14. The reply in Acts 10:15 tells him not to call impure what God has made clean. Ezekiel's defiled bread among the nations is answered by the gospel going to the nations.

Christ bore our sins in His body on the tree. Peter uses the language of bearing and of the body to say what Ezekiel's sign act could only picture. Where Ezekiel carried guilt as a sign, Christ carried it away, and by His wounds people are healed.

Christ was offered once to bear the sins of many, and will appear a second time not to bear sin but to bring salvation. The 'once' stands against the repeated days of Ezekiel's lying, 4:5-6. The sacrifice that ends all bearing makes the reappearance one of salvation.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's opening chapters ended with a man and woman driven east from the garden because they listened to a voice other than God's. Ezekiel 4 and 5 is the same story at national scale. A people brought into a land, given statutes and set in the center of the nations, have repeated Adam's sin, and now they are driven east again. The brick city under siege is Eden's gate shut a second time, with a sword behind the exiles as it was behind the first pair. The very verb of Leviticus 26:33, the drawn sword that follows the scattered, is the sword of 5:2 and 5:12.

The passage answers what the covenant had warned in Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28. Those chapters were set out like a treaty, blessings for faithfulness and curses for covenant breaking, and Israel had ignored the fine print. Ezekiel does not add anything new; he reads the curses aloud, with props. The prophetic office throughout the Old Testament is the work of reminding a people of what they already knew, and this section does it with the most costly means available.

The passage also sets up what follows. Chapter 6 takes the same threat to the high places, chapter 7 declares the end, chapter 8 shows the temple's corruption, and chapters 9 to 11 describe the glory leaving the city. And it plants the hope: a few hairs in the garment, 5:3, a remnant, 6:8, and, much later, a land restored and a new heart, 36:24-28. The scattering is not the last chapter. God scatters so that He can gather.

The story reaches its center when the true Bearer of iniquity appears. Jesus is led outside the city, bears sin in His body, and takes the curse of the covenant, Galatians 3:13, so that the siege and the sword fall on Him rather than on those who trust Him. Then the temple is not rebuilt in stone but in people, 1 Corinthians 3:16-17.

In the new creation the images of this section are reversed. The famine becomes a feast, the water measured out by the cup becomes the river of life, and the city once besieged is the city whose gates are never shut, Revelation 21:25. Nothing in it is unclean, Revelation 21:27, and the God who said 'I Myself am against you' says instead, 'I will dwell with them,' Revelation 21:3.

sermon.title: Divine Judgment and Symbolism: An Analysis of Ezekiel 4-5
sermon.why: Carson works verse by verse through these sign acts, explaining the siege drama, the bound days of bearing iniquity, and the shaved hair, and showing how they dramatize the certainty of coming judgment on Jerusalem.

quiz.q: What did Ezekiel draw on the brick, and what did he then do to it?

options.text: He drew the temple and offered sacrifices on the brick.
options.note: The brick pictures the besieged city, not temple sacrifice.

options.text: He drew the city of Jerusalem and laid symbolic siege against it.
options.note: Ezekiel 4:1-3 describes drawing Jerusalem and building a miniature siege against it.

options.text: He drew a map of the exile route to Babylon.
options.note: The sign is a besieged city, not a travel map.

options.text: Nothing; the brick was left blank as a sign of emptiness.
options.note: The brick is specifically drawn with the city and besieged.

quiz.q: What did lying on his left side and then his right side represent?

options.text: A period of rest before his ministry began.
options.note: The posture was arduous and symbolic, not restful.

options.text: Mourning for his own family alone.
options.note: The bearing of iniquity concerns Israel and Judah, not his family.

options.text: Bearing the iniquity of the house of Israel, then of the house of Judah, day for year.
options.note: Ezekiel 4:4-6 explains both postures this way.

options.text: Two different prophetic visions unrelated to iniquity.
options.note: Both postures are explicitly tied to bearing iniquity.

quiz.q: Why was Ezekiel troubled about baking his bread over human excrement?

options.text: Because he had never defiled himself by eating anything unclean.
options.note: Ezekiel 4:14 records his protest on grounds of ritual purity.

options.text: Because God had not explained the sign to him.
options.note: God had explained it; his concern was personal purity.

options.text: Because he had no fuel available at all.
options.note: His objection was about defilement, not lack of fuel.

options.text: He raised no objection.
options.note: He explicitly protests in verse 14.

quiz.q: What did the three portions of shaved hair in chapter 5 represent?

options.text: Nothing specific; it was purely a fashion statement.
options.note: Each portion is directly interpreted as a form of coming judgment.

options.text: Three different kings who would rule Jerusalem.
options.note: The division pictures the fate of the people, not a king list.

options.text: Three tribes being reunited.
options.note: The sign pictures judgment and scattering, not reunification.

options.text: A third of the people dying by plague and famine, a third by the sword, and a third scattered to the wind.
options.note: Ezekiel 5:2 and 5:12 interpret the divided hair this way.

quiz.q: Why does God say Jerusalem's judgment will be unprecedented?

options.text: Because she is smaller than the surrounding nations.
options.note: Size is not the issue; the issue is the severity of her rebellion.

options.text: Because the surrounding nations pressured God to judge her.
options.note: The judgment flows from Jerusalem's own rebellion, not outside pressure.

options.text: Because she has rebelled against His ordinances more wickedly than the surrounding nations.
options.note: Ezekiel 5:6-9 gives this as the reason for judgment worse than ever done before.

options.text: There is no stated reason for the severity.
options.note: The text explicitly gives Jerusalem's exceptional rebellion as the reason.

questions: Ezekiel's body became a walking sermon long before he preached a word. Where might God be asking you to embody a truth in costly action rather than simply speak about it?

Jerusalem's judgment came because she had been given more light than the nations around her yet rebelled further. Where has God given you unusual privilege or knowledge, and how seriously are you taking the responsibility that comes with it?
Ezekiel bore Israel's iniquity in symbol; Christ bore it in reality. How does resting in what Christ actually accomplished on the cross change the way you carry guilt over your own past sin?
God measured out both judgment and mercy with exact care, by thirds, by years, by weight. How does knowing God's discipline is precise rather than random help you trust Him in a hard season?
The sign acts were humiliating and physically costly for Ezekiel to perform. What is it costing you, practically, to be faithful to what God has asked of you right now?

translationNotes.note: The mixture of wheat, barley, beans, lentils, millet, and spelt into one bread pictures the scarcity of a besieged city, where whatever grain remains must be combined rather than used separately.

Baking bread over dried human excrement, later mercifully changed to cow dung, symbolizes the ritual defilement and desperate conditions Israel would face eating unclean food among the nations of exile.

The threefold division by plague and famine, sword, and scattering to the wind matches almost exactly the historical account of Jerusalem's fall in 2 Kings 25, where famine, the sword, and exile all featured.
